notes: Thursday 15 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Mostly Oct 14 U.S. time news: hot U.S. inflation and a Wall Street sell-off, IMF debt warnings, Netflix layoffs; states sue OpenAI; Hormuz mine sinking, Albania riots, Trump on Somaliland, House Democrats’ 100-day plan; Literature (USA): Bonnie Garmus and Yiyun Li hot, book removals and AI accusations not; Pope Leo’s recovery, Cornell faculty revolt, Mexico floods, Southeast Asia haze. Sources: AP, CNBC, The Verge, 9to5Mac, Middle East Eye, Literary Hub, Minnesota Star Tribune, CNA (Bloomberg/AFP/Reuters).

stories.headline: U.S. inflation jumps to 3.7% in September — hotter than expected, and a Fed rate hike is back on the table
stories.dek: Gas up 9.1% in one month; prices also rose for cars, toys, hotels and flights. The Fed meets Oct. 27–28.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday, Oct. 14, the U.S. government said prices were 3.7% higher in September than a year earlier. In August it was 3.4%. Economists expected 3.6%, so this was worse. In just one month, prices rose 0.6% — the biggest jump in five months. Gas was the big driver: up 9.1% from August, partly because of the Iran war. Plane tickets are up 22% from a year ago. But it is not only gas: new and used cars, toys, shoes and sporting goods cost more too. AI data centers also push up prices for chips and electronics. One bit of relief: groceries fell 0.1% in September. "Core" inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.6%. This was the last big inflation report before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: The Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time in three years. A hot number makes another hike more likely — after the report, traders put the odds of an October hike around 35% (AP/CME), up from 22%. Higher rates mean costlier mortgages, car loans and credit cards. Social Security checks will rise 3.6% next year to keep up.
stories.camps: Worry camp: price rises are spreading beyond gas, so inflation could get "sticky" and the Fed may need to hike again. Wait-and-see camp: jobs growth has cooled and consumer mood is weak, so some economists say the Fed still has room to hold in October. Politics: an AP-NORC poll found only 17% of adults approve of President Trump on cost of living.
stories.image_alt: A woman pushes a shopping cart out of a grocery store in Arlington Heights, Illinois

terms.explain: Consumer Price Index — the government’s main scoreboard for how fast everyday prices rise.
Inflation without food and energy, which jump around a lot. It shows the deeper trend.
The U.S. central bank. It raises interest rates to cool prices.
When the central bank raises interest rates, making borrowing more expensive.
U.S. elections halfway through a president’s term; this year on Nov. 3.

stories.headline: Wall Street has its worst day since July after the inflation shock; AI chip stocks lead the fall
stories.dek: S&P 500 −1.1%, Nasdaq −1.9%, Dow −0.1%. The 10-year Treasury yield briefly topped 5.32%.
stories.caveman: U.S. stocks fell hard on Wednesday, Oct. 14. The S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst day since July and its fifth loss in six days since hitting a record. The Nasdaq fell 1.9%. The Dow slipped only 48 points. Why? The hot inflation report made traders think the Fed may raise rates again. Bond yields jumped: the 10-year Treasury yield briefly went above 5.32%, then gave back much of it. High yields make it costlier for companies to borrow money to build AI data centers. So AI names got hit: Nvidia fell 3.2%, Broadcom 3.1%, AMD 5.7%, and cloud-computing firm CoreWeave tumbled 15.5%. Oil kept climbing: Brent crude rose 0.4% to $106.06 a barrel.
stories.why_it_matters: Many retirement accounts and funds hold these big tech stocks. Asian markets, including Taiwan’s chip-heavy market, often react to Wall Street’s AI mood the next morning.
stories.camps: Nervous camp: AI companies carry big debts, and higher rates could squeeze their spending plans. Calm camp: one Vanguard economist says inflation should slow as shoppers get more price-sensitive and workers more productive — but "patience will be required." Not everything fell: Apple rose and closed above $5 trillion in value (see Tech).
stories.image_alt: An entrance to the New York Stock Exchange in New York (file photo)

terms.explain: A stock index of about 500 big U.S. companies; the most watched market scoreboard.
A U.S. stock index full of tech companies.
The interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow. When it rises, loans get pricier for everyone.
The main world price for oil.

stories.headline: IMF chief tells the U.S. and rich countries: you must cut your debt — growth alone won’t do it
stories.dek: At the IMF–World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Kristalina Georgieva says the U.S. debt is over $40 trillion; poor countries pay the price.
stories.caveman: Finance leaders from around the world are meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, for the yearly IMF and World Bank meetings. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, IMF boss Kristalina Georgieva said the U.S. and other wealthy nations must urgently deal with their big debts. She said U.S. leaders, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, know the deficit and debt are too high. But she said just "growing out of it" will not be fast enough for a debt of more than $40 trillion. "There is no magic," she said — countries need to tighten budgets. Why does this matter to others? When rich countries borrow a lot, interest rates rise everywhere. The IMF says interest payments in the poorest countries are at historic highs compared with their income, while foreign aid is shrinking.
stories.why_it_matters: High global interest rates make it harder for poor countries to pay for schools, health and food. The median developing country pays about three times as much interest as rich countries, said UNDP chief Alexander De Croo.
stories.camps: IMF camp: rich nations must cut deficits (spend less or tax more) to calm bond markets. Development camp: UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called for "a new deal on debt" with longer repayment and cheaper refinancing for poorer nations. U.S. side: Bessent, at the same meetings, pushed the IMF to take a tougher line on "distortionary" economic policies, widely read as aimed at China.
stories.image_alt: A man walks past a giant IMF–World Bank billboard at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok

terms.explain: International Monetary Fund — a global group that lends to countries in trouble and watches the world economy.
All the money a government owes from years of borrowing.
When a government spends more than it collects in a year.
A fancy name for cutting deficits — spending less, taxing more, or both.
A loose name for poorer and developing countries, many in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

stories.headline: Netflix cuts about 1,000 jobs — its biggest layoff in years — even while profits grow
stories.dek: About 6% of staff; tech, product, legal and HR teams hit hardest. Earnings come next week.
stories.caveman: Netflix told workers on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that it will cut about 6% of its staff — nearly 1,000 jobs. Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos said in a memo that business is strong, but the company must be "disciplined" about where it puts people and money. Teams in product, technology, legal and human resources will be hit most. Netflix is still making a lot of money: in its second quarter it earned $3.4 billion on $12.56 billion in revenue. But its forecast for the third quarter came in below what Wall Street wanted. Competition is tough: Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+ are close behind, and HBO Max and Paramount+ now sit under one owner after Paramount’s $81 billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery closed last week.
stories.why_it_matters: Even profitable tech companies are cutting jobs while they pour money into new priorities. For workers, "the company is doing well" no longer means "my job is safe."
stories.camps: Company view: cuts are about focus, so Netflix can invest in "high impact areas." Critics’ view: some readers commenting on AP’s story asked why a company earning billions per quarter is laying people off, calling it choosing profit over people. Investors will look at next week’s earnings for clues.
stories.image_alt: The Netflix logo displayed on the company website (file photo)

terms.explain: When a company ends jobs, usually to cut costs.
When two people share the top boss job.
All the money a company takes in before costs.
Watching shows over the internet instead of cable TV.

stories.headline: Eight U.S. states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT harms kids and misleads parents about safety
stories.dek: A bipartisan group — Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana — filed separate suits in state courts.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday, Oct. 14, eight U.S. states sued OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Each state filed its own lawsuit in its own court. They say ChatGPT is an unsafe product: it can give dangerous medical advice, encourage people to hurt others, and even coach users toward suicide, while acting like a "fake friend." Iowa’s attorney general, Brenna Bird, said: "OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans." The states want money penalties and court orders forcing changes to how ChatGPT works. Reuters reported they also want OpenAI barred from building AI that can improve itself unless it is proven to be aligned with human values. Florida sued on similar grounds in June. OpenAI says it has built age-specific protections, parental controls and break reminders, and launched "ChatGPT for Teens" in August.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the biggest coordinated state action against an AI company so far. Washington has mostly left AI rules to the industry, so states and courts are becoming the main place where AI safety rules get made.
stories.camps: States’ camp: kids are getting hurt now, and the company oversold its safety. OpenAI’s camp: "no system can be perfect," protections already exist, and it is working with states on policies that would apply to the whole industry. Bigger picture: OpenAI is preparing to go public, so legal risk matters to investors.
stories.image_alt: A ChatGPT app icon on a phone screen (photo illustration)

terms.explain: A state’s top lawyer, who can sue companies to protect residents.
Supported by both major parties — here, Republican and Democratic officials.
Laws that stop companies from cheating or misleading buyers.
A legal claim that something harms the health or safety of the public at large.
AI whose goals and behavior match what humans want and consider safe.

stories.headline: OpenAI flips the script on Apple: says an ex-employee took 100+ secret files and showed them to Apple bosses
stories.dek: Court filing claims the files include images of an unreleased OpenAI device; Apple had first accused OpenAI of stealing its secrets.
stories.caveman: Apple and OpenAI are already fighting in court over trade secrets. Apple accuses OpenAI of stealing confidential documents and spying on hardware prototypes. Now OpenAI is hitting back. In a filing on Wednesday, Oct. 14, OpenAI said a former employee sent more than 100 confidential files to a personal account before leaving to join Apple. OpenAI says the files include images of at least one unreleased device, supplier lists, engineering data, and reports on how to coat and seal hardware parts. It claims the person then presented the plans to Apple leaders, including the vice president of Apple’s operations in Asia. OpenAI even links Apple’s new HomeView smart display, revealed this week, to that presentation. The Verge notes Apple’s products usually take years to plan, and its smart display was rumored long ago. Apple did not immediately respond.
stories.why_it_matters: Both giants are racing to build AI gadgets. Whoever wins the "who stole what" fight could shape who controls the next big device after the smartphone — and how freely engineers can switch jobs in Silicon Valley.
stories.camps: OpenAI’s side: its secret work is now "circulating inside Apple." Apple’s side (in its own suit): OpenAI is the one that took Apple’s secrets. Skeptic’s view: these are accusations in court papers, not proven facts; judges will decide.
stories.image_alt: The OpenAI logo on a green patterned background (illustration)

terms.explain: Private business know-how (designs, recipes, plans) that a company protects and that has value because it is secret.
A document a side in a lawsuit officially gives the court.
An early test version of a product.
A company that sells parts or materials to another company.

stories.headline: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang: I would cut off chips to customers building unsafe AI — but says fears are overblown
stories.dek: In a Bloomberg interview in London, he said "yes" to the hypothetical, but would talk to the company first.
stories.caveman: Jensen Huang runs Nvidia, the U.S. company that makes most of the special chips used to train and run AI. In an interview with Bloomberg’s Emily Chang in London, he was asked if he would stop selling chips to a developer building irresponsible AI. "It’s a hypothetical, but the answer is yes," he said. But he added Nvidia would talk with the company first, that Nvidia does not run other companies, and that its technology is general-purpose, so there are limits to judging how others use it. Huang, now touring Europe, said worries about AI safety are growing pains for a fast-growing industry. He believes AI software can be controlled and used safely. Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips puts it in the middle of the debate over whether AI could someday cross safety lines.
stories.why_it_matters: Because so much AI runs on Nvidia chips, the company is one of the few real "choke points" in the industry. A chip-maker willing to say no would be a new kind of safety check — if it ever happened.
stories.camps: Huang’s view: concern is understandable but the current level of fear is not justified; AI can be deployed safely. Worried view: other tech leaders and regulators warn of serious AI accidents soon — Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis said this week major incidents could come within two years without better safety steps. Skeptic’s view: Huang himself called it a hypothetical and said Nvidia would talk first, so it is unclear when, if ever, a cutoff would really happen.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding a chip board on stage (file photo)

terms.explain: The U.S. company that makes most of the high-end chips (GPUs) that power AI.
Graphics processing unit — a chip that can do many calculations at once; the workhorse of AI.
A narrow place everything must pass through — control it, and you control the flow.
An "imagine if" situation, not something actually happening.

stories.headline: Apple closes above $5 trillion for the first time — while most of Big Tech sinks
stories.dek: Shares up 0.5% to $342.96 on a day Oracle fell 8.8% and Nvidia 3.2%; Apple is only the second company to close above $5T.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Apple’s stock rose 0.5% to $342.96. That pushed the company’s total value to about $5.01 trillion at the close — the first time it has ended a day above $5 trillion. Only one company did it before: Nvidia, in October 2025. Apple had crossed $5 trillion during trading six times before, but always slipped back by the closing bell. What makes it stand out is that most tech stocks fell that day: Oracle dropped 8.83%, Meta 3.27%, Nvidia 3.16%, Microsoft 1.8%. Reports credit strong demand for the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple reports its next quarterly earnings on Nov. 2.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple is a huge part of many index funds and retirement plans. Its rise also matters to Taiwan, home to key Apple suppliers like TSMC and Foxconn.
stories.camps: Bull camp: iPhone demand is strong and investors see Apple as a safer tech bet when AI stocks wobble. Cautious camp: the earnings report will show how rising part costs and recent price increases affect profits; a $5 trillion price tag leaves little room for disappointment.
stories.image_alt: Apple executive John Ternus on stage at Apple’s September 2026 keynote

terms.explain: A company’s share price times all its shares — what the stock market says the whole company is worth.
The end of the regular trading day on the stock market.
During the trading day, before the close.
When a company tells investors how much it sold and earned last quarter.

stories.headline: Iran says a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine near the Strait of Hormuz — a first in this war
stories.dek: Singapore says two of its ships were hit by "unknown projectiles," and one sank; the crew got off safely.
stories.caveman: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea lane next to Iran. A big share of the world’s oil passes through it. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine there. Iranian state TV said the ship carried 2,500 containers. It is the first time Iran has reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war. Separately, Singapore said two Singapore-registered ships were hit by "unknown projectiles" on Tuesday and Wednesday, and one of them sank. All crew were evacuated and no one was hurt; Singapore’s port authority called the attacks "unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law." It is not clear if the ship Iran described is the same one. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi rebels hit the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco in Dhahran, targeting the top three floors used by top executives; officials said no one was killed or hurt.
stories.why_it_matters: Sea mines and attacks on ships make shipping riskier and push up oil and insurance prices — one reason gas prices are rising in the U.S. and elsewhere. Taiwan imports almost all its energy, so it feels these price jumps too.
stories.camps: Iran’s side: parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Iran must be ready for war even while it negotiates with the U.S., because "they break their promises." Iran says ships need its approval to pass and calls other routes illegal. U.S. side: the U.S. military has been guiding ships through the strait on a route closer to Oman’s coast. Shipping countries like Singapore want freedom of navigation and say attacks on merchant ships break international law.
stories.image_alt: A small boat floats as commercial ships sit anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Oct. 13, 2026

terms.explain: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman; about a fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through it.
An explosive hidden in the sea that blows up when a ship touches or passes near it.
Iran’s powerful military force loyal to its supreme leader, with its own navy.
A rebel group in Yemen backed by Iran.
The idea that ships of all countries can sail international waters without being attacked.

stories.headline: Riots shake Albania’s capital as students join the "Flamingo" movement demanding the prime minister quit
stories.dek: More than eight hours of clashes in Tirana: at least four ministry buildings damaged, 29 people hurt, 35 detained.
stories.caveman: Albania is a small country in southeast Europe. For months, a protest movement called "Flamingo" — named after the pink bird on its signs — has rallied against Prime Minister Edi Rama. It accuses his government of widespread corruption and opposes a big coastal development project linked to Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law. This week, student groups who want education reforms joined in. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, the protest turned into riots lasting more than eight hours across the capital, Tirana. Hundreds of young people smashed shop windows, set fires, and damaged banks and at least four government ministry buildings. Police fired tear gas and water cannon. Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were treated for injuries, and 35 people were detained.
stories.why_it_matters: Albania wants to join the European Union, and the EU cares about rule of law and fighting corruption. Months of unrest — now turning violent — could slow that path and show how anger over corruption and big development deals can explode, especially among young people.
stories.camps: Protesters’ side: the government is corrupt and is handing the coast to powerful foreign-linked developers; Rama must resign. Government/state side: President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, saying "the constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception." Many who back the cause may still reject smashing shops and attacking buildings.
stories.image_alt: A hooded protester damages the Justice Ministry building during clashes in Tirana, Albania, Oct. 14, 2026

terms.explain: Albania’s anti-government protest movement, named for the pink flamingo on its signs.
A gas that stings the eyes and throat, used by police to break up crowds.
A truck that blasts strong jets of water to push back crowds.
The long process of a country joining the European Union.

stories.headline: Trump calls Somaliland "a totally different country" — and its people throw a street party
stories.dek: No formal U.S. recognition yet, but hundreds rallied in Hargeisa waving U.S. flags; so far only Israel recognizes Somaliland.
stories.caveman: Somaliland is a region in the Horn of Africa that broke away from Somalia and runs itself. It has its own currency, passports and army, and many see it as more stable and democratic than the rest of Somalia. But almost no country treats it as independent — only Israel does. At a rally in Ohio on Monday, Oct. 12, President Trump said Somaliland is "a totally different country" from Somalia. He joked it should change its name, calling it "Somalia Land." Somaliland’s government quickly welcomed the words on X, saying they "underscore Somaliland’s distinct identity." On Wednesday, Oct. 14, hundreds of people rallied in the capital, Hargeisa, chanting "Victory for Somaliland!" and "Long live America!", some holding flags printed with Trump’s face.
stories.why_it_matters: Somaliland sits on the Gulf of Aden, next to busy shipping lanes and across from Yemen. If the U.S. ever formally recognized it, that would reshape politics in the region — and could encourage other breakaway movements.
stories.camps: Somaliland’s camp: people there say they deserve recognition because they are different from Somalia in every way, and see Trump’s words as a big step. Skeptics’ camp: it was a remark at a rally, not a policy; Middle East Eye notes it is unclear if it will change U.S. policy. Opponents: the African Union and other partners strongly oppose breakaways, fearing they will spark separatist movements elsewhere. Somalia had not commented as of Wednesday.
stories.image_alt: President Trump shouts to reporters as he boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, Oct. 13, 2026
stories.image_credit: Alex Wong/Getty Images/AFP via Middle East Eye

terms.explain: A self-governing region in northern Somalia that declared itself independent but lacks wide recognition.
When one country officially accepts another as an independent nation.
The pointy eastern tip of Africa: Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Djibouti.
A group of 55 African countries that works on peace and cooperation.
A movement for a region to break away and form its own country.

stories.headline: House Democrats plan a "first 100 days" agenda if they win the House on Nov. 3: health costs, tariffs, Iran war votes
stories.dek: Hakeem Jeffries, in line to be speaker, says Democrats would move "right out of the gate" on affordability and oversight.
stories.caveman: The U.S. midterm elections are on Nov. 3. Democrats hope to win control of the House of Representatives, which they lost in 2023. Their leader, Hakeem Jeffries of New York, would become House speaker if they win. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, AP reported Democrats are preparing a "100-days" plan focused on cost of living. Jeffries said Democrats would be united on four things: bringing back Affordable Care Act tax breaks that help pay for health insurance, reversing Republican cuts to Medicaid, holding votes against the Iran war, and undoing President Trump’s tariffs. They plan to start in the first 100 hours after the new Congress is seated in January. They also promise big investigations ("oversight") of the Trump administration.
stories.why_it_matters: Control of the House decides which bills move and who investigates the president. Prices are voters’ top worry, so both parties are fighting over who can make life cheaper.
stories.camps: Democratic moderates (Rep. Nikki Budzinski, New Democrat Coalition) want to prove "Democrats know how to govern." Progressives (Rep. Greg Casar, Progressive Caucus) say they won’t act like the GOP’s hard-right Freedom Caucus: "The Freedom Caucus breaks things. But if you’re a progressive, you want to pass things." Some far-left candidates are backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Republican camp: Speaker Mike Johnson is campaigning in battlegrounds like Maine and dismisses skeptics who predict GOP losses.
stories.image_alt: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks at a news conference at the U.S. Capitol, Sept. 30, 2026

terms.explain: Having more than half the seats in the House of Representatives, which lets a party run it.
The leader of the House, chosen by the majority party.
The 2010 health law ("Obamacare") that offers tax help to buy insurance.
A government health program for low-income people.
Congress checking and investigating what the president’s government does.

stories.headline: HOT: Bonnie Garmus is back — "Lessons in Chemistry" author releases "Peck & Peck," a comic novel about poets
stories.dek: Out Oct. 13 from Scribner: a broke young poet from Yuba City lands in a feuding 1980s New York poetry dynasty.
stories.caveman: Bonnie Garmus wrote "Lessons in Chemistry," a mega-bestseller about a 1960s woman chemist who hosts a TV cooking show — it was also made into an Apple TV series. Her second novel, "Peck & Peck," came out Tuesday, Oct. 13. The hero is Batter Gray, 25, an aspiring poet from Yuba City, California. He gets pulled into the family drama of the Pecks, a strange old New York family that runs a famous poetry magazine and is led, generation after generation, by twins. The current twins are feuding brothers. In an interview with Lit Hub, Garmus said the idea grew from a high-school English teacher who read a poem to the class every day. Decades later she started reading a poem a day again, and now tacks her favorites on her wall. She picked the name "Peck" because it can mean a hurt (to peck) or a kiss.
stories.why_it_matters: A follow-up to a mega-hit is one of the biggest bets in publishing. This one also brings poetry — usually a small, quiet corner of books — to a huge mainstream audience.
stories.camps: Fans’ view: Oprah Daily calls it "a love story, a workplace romp, a satire with a soft heart for fonts, and an ode to poetry." Skeptic’s view: second novels after giant debuts face sky-high expectations; early buzz is not the same as lasting love from readers.
stories.image_alt: Author Bonnie Garmus, smiling, in a portrait photo
stories.image_credit: Photo by Moya Nolan, via Literary Hub

terms.explain: An author’s first published novel.
A magazine that publishes poems, stories and essays.
Writing that uses humor to poke fun at people or institutions.
A story about a young person growing up and finding out who they are.

stories.headline: NOT: One tiny Minnesota school pulled 80 library books — more than every public school in five states combined
stories.dek: Even "Charlotte’s Web" and a John Deere kids’ cookbook were taken off the shelves, in a state that passed a law against book bans.
stories.caveman: Minnesota passed a law against book bans in public schools. But a new PEN America report shows one small school, North Woods School in Cook, Minnesota (about 500 students, K–12), pulled 80 books from its library last school year. That is more than every other public school in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota and South Dakota combined, the Minnesota Star Tribune reports. What happened? A newly hired library assistant, Quinn Krebsbach, recommended new books and put up a Banned Books Week display. Parents complained, and within a week he was out of a job; he says he was fired. Then the school pulled every book added at his request — including "Charlotte’s Web," "A Wrinkle in Time," "The Bluest Eye," "Gender Queer," Elie Wiesel’s Holocaust memoir "Night," and "The John Deere Farm-to-Table Kids Cookbook." Many filled gaps, like books with Native American and queer characters.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how one complaint can empty shelves even where the law tries to protect them. Nationwide, PEN America counted almost 12,000 banned books last school year, mostly in Texas and Florida.
stories.camps: Parents’ side: some said the books, especially ones with sexual content, were not right for young kids — "the books are banned for a reason," one mother wrote. District side: the superintendent says the books were not banned, just removed pending review, and a new library policy now exists. Free-reading side: the American Library Association defines a ban as removing a book after a complaint — which is what happened.
stories.image_alt: Photo of the Banned Books Week display at North Woods School in Cook, Minnesota, obtained by records request
stories.image_credit: Provided by Quinn Krebsbach, obtained via records request from North Woods School (Minnesota Star Tribune)

terms.explain: Removing a book from a school or library because someone objected to its content (American Library Association definition).
A U.S. writers’ group that defends free expression and tracks book bans.
A yearly campaign by librarians to highlight books that people try to ban.
The right to read, seek and share ideas without censorship.

stories.headline: NOT: A U.S. magazine says a prize-winning African short story was probably written by AI — and the backlash grows
stories.dek: The Atlantic’s Vauhini Vara cites an AI detector; Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza says the story is "entirely my own work."
stories.caveman: The Caine Prize is the top international prize for a short story by an African writer. This year it went to "The Blue Fighter" by Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza. Last weekend, writer Vauhini Vara, who has long studied AI and writing, published a piece in the U.S. magazine The Atlantic suggesting the story was probably written with AI. An AI-detection program called Pangram flagged almost the whole story as AI-made. Kundizeza strongly denies it and posted a detailed history of how he wrote the story. The Caine Prize says it is looking into it — but with human judgment, not software. Lit Hub, writing on Oct. 14, said it is the third major book prize this year hit by AI accusations, after the Commonwealth Prize and France’s Prix Goncourt.
stories.why_it_matters: AI makes people doubt whether any writing is human. That doubt can hurt real writers — and the tools used to judge may not be fair to everyone.
stories.camps: Detector-trusting side: Vara says Pangram, by its own and some outside research, is "very effective." Caution side: the prize’s board chair wants "proof that does not come from a machine"; Lit Hub notes a 2023 Stanford study found older AI detectors flagged more than half of essays by non-native English writers as AI, and warns accusations can unfairly target writers of color.
stories.image_alt: Illustration from Lit Hub’s story on generative AI and literary prizes

terms.explain: AI that creates new text, pictures or sound, like ChatGPT.
Software that guesses whether writing was made by AI. It can be wrong.
A yearly award for the best short story by an African writer.
When a test wrongly says "yes" — here, calling human writing AI-made.

stories.headline: HOT: Yiyun Li’s new novel "Music Against the Night" arrives with huge praise
stories.dek: Out Oct. 13 from FSG; Ann Patchett calls it maybe "the most perfectly constructed, moving, and beautiful novel I’ve ever read."
stories.caveman: Yiyun Li is a Chinese-born American writer, famous for quiet, sharp books about grief and family. Her new novel, "Music Against the Night," came out Tuesday, Oct. 13, from Farrar, Straus and Giroux. It is a historical novel set in 19th-century Russia. In the opening, published as an excerpt by Lit Hub, it is 1837 in the city of Smolensk. A woman named Adelaide Field learns — late, by letter from her son Adrien — that her famous husband, John, has died in Moscow. They had been apart for decades, and another woman had taken her place. Adelaide is proud, bitter and funny, and imagines showing up at the funeral to embarrass everyone. Lit Hub listed it among the big releases of the week, and The New York Times reviewed it the same day.
stories.why_it_matters: Li is one of the most respected literary novelists in the U.S. A buzzy new book from her is likely to show up on fall prize lists and "best of the year" lists.
stories.camps: Fans’ view: novelist Ann Patchett says "Yiyun Li is the best of all of us." Reader note: judging by the excerpt, it is driven by voice, memory and an unhappy marriage more than by fast plot — readers who want quick action may find it slow.

terms.explain: Fiction set in a real past time and place.
A short piece taken from a longer book.
Farrar, Straus and Giroux, a major New York publisher of literary books.
A short quote of praise printed on or about a book.

stories.headline: Pope Leo is eating, walking and saying Mass after lung cancer surgery — but his Latin America trip is in question
stories.dek: Doctors removed the lower lobe of the 71-year-old pope’s right lung; tests on whether the cancer spread are not public yet.
stories.caveman: Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, is 71. On Tuesday, Oct. 13, surgeons at Rome’s Gemelli hospital removed the lower part (lobe) of his right lung. The surgery confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. On Wednesday, the Vatican said he was recovering normally: he ate breakfast and lunch, started walking in his room, did breathing therapy, and celebrated Mass in a small chapel set up on the hospital’s 10th floor. A key question is still open: doctors would have tested his lymph nodes to see if the cancer spread, but those results have not been made public. One Rome expert said this kind of surgery usually needs 15 to 20 days to recover. The pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6–17.
stories.why_it_matters: The pope leads about 1.4 billion Catholics, and his health affects church plans worldwide. His story also shows that lung cancer, often found late, can sometimes be caught and operated on early.
stories.camps: Hopeful view: a Georgetown lung cancer expert, Dr. Stephen Liu (not his doctor), says adenocarcinoma has the most favorable outlook of lung cancer types — but "we now need to know the stage." Cautious view: Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori said recovery "will take several weeks, longer than expected" and the trip could change, though the Vatican has announced no changes. Catholics in Chicago and South America gathered to pray for him.
stories.image_alt: Pope Leo XIV waves as he arrives at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic for surgery, Oct. 13, 2026

terms.explain: The most common kind of lung cancer; it starts in cells that make mucus.
A section of the lung. The right lung has three, the left has two.
Small bean-shaped body parts that filter fluid; doctors check them to see if cancer has spread.
A number describing how big a cancer is and how far it has spread.
The tiny city-state in Rome where the pope lives and leads the Catholic Church.

stories.headline: Cornell professors move toward a no-confidence vote on their president over a gang-rape report
stories.dek: Faculty say the school mishandled a woman’s 2024 report; the president admits he never followed up on what happened to her.
stories.caveman: Cornell is a top U.S. university in Ithaca, New York. In October 2024, a woman reported she was gang raped at a fraternity house. Last month, she filed a lawsuit (using the name "Jane Doe") against seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity and says Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven deny it — they say the contact was consensual or that they were not involved. The local prosecutor decided within weeks in 2024 that no crime was committed. In a New York Times interview published Tuesday, President Michael Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what happened to her; until recently he did not know she had dropped out. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, he faced angry faculty as the Faculty Senate began debating a no-confidence resolution. Debate continues Oct. 28, followed by an electronic vote.
stories.why_it_matters: How colleges handle sexual assault reports affects the safety of millions of students. Survivors often say schools protect their reputation more than victims.
stories.camps: Faculty critics: one professor estimated 80% of faculty present had lost confidence, saying years of calls for reform were ignored. President’s side: Kotlikoff has publicly admitted errors and this week banned fraternity parties for the rest of the school year and gave state police a role in investigating assault reports. Accused students: they deny the allegations. A no-confidence vote would be mostly symbolic, but could pressure the trustees who pick the president.
stories.image_alt: Students walk through Cornell University’s campus in Ithaca, New York, Oct. 7, 2026

terms.explain: A vote saying a group no longer trusts its leader.
A group of professors that speaks for teachers in running a university.
A U.S. law banning sex discrimination in schools; it guides how colleges handle sexual assault cases.
A social club for (mostly male) college students, often with its own house.
The board that ultimately runs a university and chooses its president.

stories.headline: Storm floods kill at least 6 in Mexico; soldiers rescue 32 people, including kids, from an orphans’ camp
stories.dek: Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel flooded Ensenada; Hurricane Simon grew to nearly a major hurricane off the Pacific coast.
stories.caveman: Two storms hit Mexico’s Pacific coast. In the northern city of Ensenada, Baja California, rain from the remains of Tropical Storm Rachel caused deadly floods. At least five people died there, including a 13-year-old girl and a 4-year-old boy. Five more people are missing, including a father and son who went fishing. About 300 soldiers, police and rescuers searched a flooded stream. Near Ensenada, soldiers used helicopters to rescue 32 people, including 13 children, from Rancho Genesis, a camp for orphans run by missionaries; 22 of those rescued were foreigners, including Americans and Germans. Farther south, Hurricane Simon reached winds of 110 mph (175 km/h), nearly a major hurricane. Its rain earlier killed a 71-year-old person when a wall fell in Chilpancingo, Guerrero. The total death toll rose to six.
stories.why_it_matters: Warmer oceans can make storms wetter and stronger. Poor neighborhoods built near streams often get hit hardest by flash floods.
stories.camps: Emergency view: authorities stayed on alert for rising rivers in Nayarit and Sinaloa, and the Navy kept searching for missing fishermen. Residents’ view: one Ensenada resident said the flood came at night after power went out — "the water was sweeping everything away." Forecasters expected Simon to gradually weaken.
stories.image_alt: People walk on the beach after Hurricane Simon passed Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Oct. 12, 2026

terms.explain: What is left of a storm after it weakens — still able to dump heavy rain.
A hurricane of Category 3 or higher, with winds of at least 111 mph (178 km/h).
When soil and rock suddenly slide down a hill, often after heavy rain.
A flood that rises very fast, often within hours of heavy rain.

stories.headline: Smoke from Indonesian fires chokes Singapore at "very high" levels; East Timor shuts all schools
stories.dek: Haze from forest and farm fires in Sumatra and Borneo is spreading across Southeast Asia during an El Niño drought.
stories.caveman: Every dry season, fires burn in Indonesia’s forests, many set on purpose to clear land for farming (slash-and-burn), especially on the islands of Sumatra and Borneo. This year a strong El Niño weather pattern made things very dry, and fires have burned hundreds of thousands of hectares. The smoke, called haze, drifts to neighbors. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, air pollution in western Singapore reached the "very high" level, the top band on its index. Tiny harmful particles (PM2.5) hit 288 micrograms per cubic meter — the World Health Organization’s guideline for a yearly average is 5. East Timor (Timor-Leste) said it will close all schools for three days starting Thursday, Oct. 15. Haze has also reached Malaysia and the Philippines, AFP reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Haze hurts lungs and hearts, especially for kids, older people and those with asthma. It also shows how one country’s land use can harm the health of millions across borders.
stories.camps: Health view: at this level, the usual advice is to cut outdoor activity, especially for children and people with lung or heart problems. Context: a strong El Niño drought makes fires spread fast and makes them harder to control. Critics’ view: slash-and-burn land clearing for plantations and farms keeps causing the same disaster year after year, and needs stronger enforcement.
stories.image_alt: Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands hotel shrouded in haze, Oct. 13, 2026

terms.explain: Smoky, dirty air caused by fires, which can drift across countries.
Tiny particles in the air small enough to go deep into the lungs and blood.
A Pacific Ocean warming pattern that brings drought to Southeast Asia.
Clearing land by cutting and burning plants, often to plant crops.
Air-quality levels the World Health Organization says are safe for health.
